npm.integrity_format: sha512-<base64> (npm registry `integrity` field value; sha1-<base64> accepted for legacy rows)
npm.allowlist_semantics: allowlist=true = pinned and trusted (change requires human review); allowlist=false = known-untrusted, finding always; absent = unpinned, finding (severity medium)
npm.changes: any add, remove, or version/integrity bump requires a human-reviewed diff; automated update (e.g. `npm audit fix --force`, `npm update`) is forbidden unless the resulting diff passes human review

github_refs.commit_sha_format: full 40-hex (SHA-1) or 64-hex (SHA-256) commit SHA; short SHAs are invalid (moved-tag/malleable-ref defense)
github_refs.allowlist_semantics: allowlist=true = pinned and trusted (change requires human review); allowlist=false = known-untrusted, finding always; absent = unpinned or floating ref (branch/range), finding (severity high)
github_refs.changes: any add, remove, or commit_sha change requires a human-reviewed diff; `git verify-tag` is not a substitute for SHA pinning (moved tags), it is a supplement

policy.rebaseline: requires a human-reviewed diff; never auto-accepted; every re-baseline is recorded with owner, rationale, and date
human_review_covers: version intent: exact-semver pin vs floating range
integrity/provenance: registry integrity field, npm provenance (Sigstore), signed tags
install scripts: presence of postinstall/preinstall/install in the pinned version's manifest
publisher identity: npm maintainer / GitHub owner verified, not typosquat
license and declared dependencies of the pinned artifact
lockfile diff accompanying the pin change

rules.label: INJ-HOOK
rules.note: P0-1 fix: .git/hooks/** + gitdir/hooks/** route to parse (previously walked but never matched). gitdir/ is the git-trackable alias for .git/.

rules.label: INJ-PROMPT
rules.note: F-12 (blind /launch run 6, 2026-10-09): this rule read only `**/*.md`, so a prompt-injection payload in any source or config file was invisible — identical bytes gave 2 findings as payload.md and 0 as payload.js, while INJ-SECRET (path `**`) caught a real credential in src/payments.js. A scanner that cannot read source is not a security scanner. Broadened to code, config, markup and data files. Expect more findings: the cost of a blind rule is higher than the cost of a noisy one, and the residual FP classes are now visible instead of hiding behind a clean scan that proved nothing.

rules.label: INJ-OBFUSC
rules.known_fp_note: npm integrity fields (sha512-...) and lockfile hashes are legitimate base64 blobs; excluded as documented known-FP class (02f §10, Nina FP budget). Path exclusions live ONLY in the top-level known_fp_excludes block — F-9 fix 2026-08-23: the former rule-level duplicate here was dead config that had already diverged; single source of truth is top-level.
known_fp_classes: camelCase-acronym word runs joined by single / (e.g. Substitute/Combine/Adapt)
URL fragments with repeated slashes or dots (file://, raw.githubusercontent.com)
rules.note: F-3 (Victor): looksLikeBase64 guard (digit-or-symbol + mixed case + no // and no .) reduced repo-wide FPs 87 -> 3 on .agents. Remaining 3 = documented FP classes above; not suppressed further to avoid masking real blobs.

rules.label: INJ-PATH
rules.note: P1-3 narrowed: filename-scoped ONLY (walk-time rel), never content lines or interpolated identifiers. Prose $/parens are NOT findings.

rules.label: INJ-SECRET

entropy.note: P2: window is integer 8 (was '8-char sliding' string parsed by accident). threshold 2.6 (max achievable for 8 distinct chars is 3.0; 3.5 was unreachable — rule could never fire). Regex match with entropy < threshold is NOT a finding (negative fixture: AKIA + repeated chars -> ~0.0).

rules.note: F-1 (blind /launch run 2026-10-08): the branch read `sk-` with a hyphen while Stripe uses `sk_`, and the entropy check measured the fixed `sk_live_` prefix as if it were secret material — so every Stripe key in every codebase was undetectable by construction. Proven: a live Stripe key planted in src/ produced ZERO findings and the launch gate returned PASS. The sibling `ghp_` branch in this same rule already used an underscore, so the hyphen was a typo-class error. The literal key is deliberately not reproduced here: a rule table that matches its own patterns is the same class of problem as a scanner scanning its own fixtures.

rules.label: S16-BEACON
rules.note: F-4 (Victor): extended to pwsh/iex/cmd + sudo; iex is canonical PowerShell download-exec. Round-table 2026-09-08: hook paths appended (keywordless curl-pipe hooks exited 0 — extensionless hook filenames never matched the ext glob and vcsMeta skipped content rules; scanner exempts BEACON-1 from the vcsMeta guard).

fault_contract.note: Exit 2 (fail-closed) is triggered by tool/environment failure, NOT by harness-shaped content. Negative fixtures (harness-shaped unknown dirs) must exit 0.

fault_inputs.trigger: npm audit/OSV/socket.dev subprocess killed or non-zero

fp_metric.numerator: informational findings := rule hits labeled severity low OR known-FP-class (documented per-rule known-FP notes)
fp_metric.denominator: corpus files × harness shapes per run (baseline-corpus executions)
fp_metric.formula: FP rate = numerator ÷ denominator, frozen corpus only, per harness shape
fp_metric.gate: NEW-FINDINGS-ONLY vs frozen baseline; new findings labeled, never auto-baselined

known_fp_excludes.note: Path globs whose matches are documented-FP-prone; scanner must not report these paths for the listed rules (02f §10, QA F-9). Plus the scanner's own adversarial corpus (evals/security/corpus/**, evals/security/held_out/**): that content IS what every rule detects, so reporting it makes the gate fire on everything and be ignored. Measured on this repo: 14 findings, one per rule, all from the corpus. INJ-OBFUSC additionally over long filesystem PATHS: its pattern is [A-Za-z0-9+/]{40,} and an absolute macOS path matches it verbatim. Measured: 91 findings, all absolute paths in telemetry NDJSON, a comparison doc and Playwright logs — data, not obfuscation. Excluding data artefacts rather than narrowing the rule, because narrowing it would change what the adversarial corpus tests. The calibration problem is named, not hidden: the rule cannot distinguish a long path from base64.

scope.mode_note:
This repository opts into `include-list`, the fail-OPEN direction, on purpose and with one reason: it is the only repository that contains its own adversarial security fixtures (evals/security/corpus) and its own security documentation, so an exclude-list scan of the whole tree reports prose that DESCRIBES an attack as though it were one.

Every OTHER repository must use the default `exclude-list`, which fails closed: only declared excluded_trees are skipped, and any new directory is scanned until somebody deliberately excludes it. Do not copy `mode: include-list` into a product repository. Measured reason: with an inclusion allowlist, a hardcoded AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE in src/config.js was silently dropped and the scan still returned a confident answer.
what_this_is: THE PRODUCT-CODE SCOPE. A release security scan answers one question: does the code we are
shipping contain a live vulnerability? It is not a whole-repository audit, and a green
result MUST NOT be read as 'the repository passed'.
This block exists because that distinction was being fudged. A blind-run audit wired the
scanner into /launch and it reported 129 findings on this repository. Triaged individually:
every one was a false positive — 19 on the scanner's own adversarial corpus, 37 on absolute
filesystem paths that match the base64 rule, 5 reviewed test fixtures, and the remainder
prose in review documents that DESCRIBE prompt-injection attacks. None was a live defect.
The honest fix is not to suppress those findings one by one until the number reaches zero.
It is to declare what is actually being scanned, report what was not, and leave the residual
visible. `artifacts/**` is historical output — review documents, telemetry logs, memory
archives — and is not shipped code. It is out of scope, with a reason, and the scanner
prints the excluded trees on every run so nobody has to remember.

excluded_trees.reason: Historical output, not shipped code: review documents, strategy comparisons, telemetry NDJSON, and memory archives. Generated by past runs and read by no shipped surface.

Transient browser-session snapshots written by an MCP browser tool. Not shipped code, regenerated on every session, and they dominate the config-file drop count: 110 page snapshots from 2026-09-24 made every clean scan read as a disclosure the size of the codebase. Added after blind /launch run 7.
Editor-local workspace settings. Not shipped code; and a developer's local settings file can legitimately contain paths and tokens that are not secrets of the product.
Evaluation scratch trees created by audit runs. Not part of any release.
The scanner's own adversarial fixtures. They are what every rule detects; scanning them makes the gate fire on its own test material.
Held-out evaluation fixtures, same reason as the corpus.
Defines the INJ-* rule patterns as a table. A file that specifies the patterns matches them by construction, exactly like the adversarial corpus. It is a description of the defence, not the defence.

scope.known_residual:
INJ-OBFUSC cannot distinguish high-entropy base64 from a filesystem path or a slash-separated
TitleCase list. Its corpus fixture ("tz0aBaTli/A1fE9yzobOmI3i+mAYW...") and the false
positive ("Substitute/Combine/Adapt/Modify") are the same shape. Narrowing the rule would
change what the adversarial corpus tests, so it was NOT narrowed. Tracked as a rule-table
defect owned by @security-engineer, not suppressed.

INJ-PROMPT / INJ-TOOL / INJ-ROLE cannot distinguish an instruction from documentation that
quotes one. Files such as .agents/TROUBLESHOOTING.md and .agents/skills.md name injection
patterns while explaining the defence. Those files ARE in scope — they are loaded into agent
context — so they are deliberately NOT excluded. The residual is real and stays visible.
